newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: War of words over Philippine budget.
newsitem.headline: War of words over Philippine budget.

text.p: The standoff between the Philippine Senate and House of Representatives over the 1997 budget was complicated on Friday by a war of words between the two sides over a fund for national development.

Proposals by the opposition-dominated Senate to slash provisions for the country-wide development fund (CDF) in the budget by 40 percent to 720 million pesos from 1.2 billion pesos had resulted in a deadlock between the two panels of Congress on Thursday.

Senator Ernesto Herrera, the Senate Finance Committee chairman, said there was strong opposition to the CDF because it could give incumbent politicians an unfair advantage in campaigning for the next election.
Presidential elections are slated for May 1998. Half of the 24-seat Senate and the entire lower House will also be up for election.
"It (the CDF) will give an advantage to the incumbent. You're not levelling the playing field," Herrera told Reuters.
The CDF is meant to be used by legislators to fund projects in areas under their jurisdiction but newspapers say it has been misused.

The Senate also deleted 74.2 billion pesos as debt service payments from the 1997 budget since these are automatically appropriated under the law. The Senate said it feared any savings from the 1997 budget could be misused for other purposes.

Both panels are not expected to resume discussions on the budget until January since Congress is now on Christmas break. But the House said it would be willing to work on the measure next Monday and Tuesday.
"This is a collective decision by senators. We are not inclined to compromise," said Herrera.
Lawmakers in the House of Representatives were quick to react.

"The question is whether the Senate should go beyond what is mandated by the Constitution. What is provided in the Consitution is for the Senate to concur with the amendments to the (budget) version enacted by the House," House minority leader Ronaldo Zamora said in a statement.
Although the Lower House agreed to make CDF allotments completely transparent, the Senate stood firm on its decision to cut it by 40 percent.
"It's the institutional commitment of the Senate to gradually phase out the CDF," said Herrera, adding that the stance was triggered by negative public perceptions of the CDF.
Herrera said he believes the Senate has the upper hand in the dispute, since if the impasse continues there will be no provisions for the CDF in any special budget appropriations.
While the current 1996 budget would remain in effect until a new budget is passed, only funds required for regular operations would automatically be appropriated, Herrera stressed.
This does not include allotments for the CDF and infrastructure projects, he said.

"The Senate-initiated amendments are fully justified. Our budget proposal is not only fiscally prudent and transparent, but is also more in keeping with congressional power over the purse rather than the budget proposed by the House and the President," Herrera said.
